Substitute teacher accused of kicking student with disabilities: ‘The gloves were coming off’
text:
FLAGLER COUNTY, Fla. — A Florida man was arrested for allegedly kicking a student with disabilities while working as a high school substitute teacher.
A witness told Flagler County deputies that she felt uncomfortable after seeing 60-year-old Bryan Schewitz forcefully move a Matanzas High School student with disabilities into a chair while the student was experiencing a behavioral episode on Oct. 16.
That witness said she felt Schewitz was too rough with the student.
Second witness reports kick
A second witness reported seeing Schewitz kick the student, according to the Flagler County Sheriff’s Office. The witness asked Schewitz about a large mark on the student’s leg.
“He kicked me, and I kicked him, so now we’re square,” Schewitz allegedly replied.
Investigators interviewed Schewitz, who claimed he accidentally kicked the student after he arrived late to class and refused to sit to start his classwork. The student started kicking toward Schewitz, he told Flagler County deputies, leading Schewitz to stick his foot out and kick accidentally, the sheriff’s office said.
Sheriff, superintendent respond
“When adults are trusted to be working with children, especially those who require extra care because of disabilities, they are expected to be the levelheaded ones in any situation and not lose control of their temper. It is never OK for a faculty member to strike a student, especially out of anger or frustration,” Sheriff Rick Staly said.
Schewitz also claimed the student was poking other students with a pencil, so he placed his hands on his shoulders and guided him to a chair. Schewitz then allegedly sat next to the student, placed his hands on the table and told him, “The gloves were coming off.”
The student also told deputies that Schewitz kicked him, the sheriff’s office said.
“This kind of behavior will not be tolerated on our campuses,” Flagler Schools Superintendent LaShakia Moore said.
Schewitz was arrested for child abuse without great bodily harm and booked at the Sheriff Perry Hall Inmate Detention Facility before being released on a $2,500 bond.

Woman who accused students of rape says Cornell president's response made her feel 'unsupported'
text:
A woman who accused several Cornell students of raping her at a fraternity party says the university’s president questioned why she waited to report the alleged assault, leaving her feeling “unsupported and disbelieved.”
The woman’s secondhand account of Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff’s remark, which the university disputes, comes as faculty prepare for a potential vote of no confidence in the Ivy League school’s leadership. The Associated Press on Tuesday obtained a letter she sent to faculty leaders last week.
The former student’s rape allegations, detailed in a lawsuit last month, have sparked campus protests, renewed scrutiny of Cornell’s disciplinary system and led New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to appoint state Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor leading a renewed investigation of the alleged October 2024 assault.
Dispute over president’s remarks
In the letter, Jane Doe said her sorority president told her that Kotlikoff questioned why she waited until the following month to report being assaulted. The sorority leader, who spoke with Kotlikoff in November 2024, interpreted his remark as casting doubt on her story.
“President Kotlikoff’s initial response was along the lines of, ‘Why did she wait so long to report it?’ ” Jane Doe wrote in the letter. She said the conversation made her less confident that the administration could handle what happened with the sensitivity and fairness she expected.
Cornell’s dean of faculty, however, offered a different account of the conversation. In an email Tuesday to faculty senators and verified by the AP, professor Chris Schaffer said another official who was present for the conversation recalled Kotlikoff asking why bystanders had not reported the alleged assault sooner through the school’s anonymous tip line, especially because the allegations were already circulating on social media.
Schaffer said he waited to share Jane Doe’s letter with faculty senators until he could get another account of the conversation. He said he forwarded the letter to university lawyers, who passed it on to an independent team investigating Cornell’s response.
Schaffer said at a meeting last week that he was against the proposed no-confidence resolution, saying it identified no specific failures or fixes, but acknowledged faculty frustration. “The anger in our community is justified and I share it.”
Kotlikoff did not respond Tuesday to an email inquiry about Jane Doe’s letter. A statement from a university spokesperson also disputed her account of the conversation, saying Kotlikoff was asking about bystanders’ actions rather than Jane Doe.
Faculty debate no-confidence resolution
Her letter, transmitted through her attorney and first reported by The New York Times, comes as Cornell faculty consider a resolution declaring no confidence in the university administration’s ability to address what some faculty members have described as an “ongoing crisis” of sexual assault on campus.
Faculty members began debating the resolution at a meeting last Wednesday, where Kotlikoff faced pointed questions about the school’s response to sexual assault allegations and its oversight of fraternities. The Faculty Senate is expected to resume debate on Oct. 28 before holding an electronic vote.
In her letter, Jane Doe said she wanted faculty members to have information that might be relevant to their deliberations. She emphasized that she was not trying to tell them how to vote.
“My intention is not to prescribe how the Senate should interpret this account, but rather to provide information that its members may wish to consider or investigate further,” she wrote.
Messages seeking comment were left for Jane Doe’s lawyers, Thomas Giuffra and W. Whitney Seals.
Noah Tamarkin, an anthropology professor and co-sponsor of the no-confidence resolution, said Tuesday he was still processing Jane Doe’s letter, but that it reinforced his belief that Cornell needs fundamental changes to rebuild trust.
“I continue to feel that the current administration hasn’t yet shown the capacity to do this,” Tamarkin wrote in a text message.
He said what stood out was Jane Doe’s account of how the conversation affected her and the apparent lack of a clear way for her to be heard or receive support.
“We need leadership that understands how much that matters,” Tamarkin wrote.
Also Tuesday, the former Justice Department official leading Cornell’s independent investigation, Sally Yates, sent a letter to the university community outlining the scope of her review, which she said is expansive.
In addition to conducting a detailed examination of Cornell’s response to Jane Doe’s allegations, Yates wrote that her team is reviewing the university’s sexual harassment and assault prevention and discipline practices, the role of campus police and other law enforcement agencies, the supervision of fraternities and sororities, and oversight by university leadership, including its board of trustees.
“We understand that some may be skeptical of our independence — I assure you that our independence is not a formality,” Yates wrote. The university, she said, has pledged complete autonomy and the resources “an independent review of this significance needs and deserves.”
“We will follow the facts wherever they lead with unwavering candor and principled judgment so that this community — and the public — can have confidence in the integrity of our findings,” Yates, the former deputy attorney general, added.

title: Bobby Charles turns unfounded claims about Hannah Pingree into a museum-style exhibit
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Lamps flickered off and on around a dinner table decorated with autumn-themed placemats and mock Maine electricity bills approaching $1,500.
On another table sat two massive mason jars, one stuffed with fake cash labeled as Democratic gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree’s “money from Augusta lobbyists” and the other empty to represent lobbyist donations to her Republican gubernatorial opponent, Bobby Charles.
The mix of tongue-in-cheek humor and unfounded allegations of nefarious self-dealing and conflicts of interest was a hallmark of the makeshift museum exhibit Charles staged in a Bangor storefront on Tuesday morning. That humor has been a fixture of his social media- and AI-driven campaign.
“Corruption: The Exhibit” marked Charles’ latest attempt to shake up a race in which he’s trailed Pingree in every poll and has received little outside help from national Republicans, after a contentious primary that drew sharp criticism from within his own party.
“Typically where there’s smoke, there’s fire,” he told reporters.
After sitting alone to watch a bit of an ad-style documentary on a TV linking Pingree and outgoing Gov. Janet Mills to the state’s economic struggles and admiring anti-Pingree charts and posters alongside cardboard cutouts of Pingree and Mills, Charles repeated claims he leveled during the last two televised debates.
They center on an $840,000 forgivable loan from MaineHousing to North Haven Sustainable Housing, a nonprofit on Pingree’s home island now led by her husband, filmmaker Jason Mann. He made the case that the wealthy island did not need such an influx of funds when other islands and communities were struggling.
Charles has also claimed without evidence that Pingree’s former office gave almost $38,000 to the Island Institute, a Rockland-based nonprofit, for a climate film produced by Mann. But the candidate has acknowledged that public records have not tied either of the grants to Mann.
He said Tuesday that he was not aware of any Republican lawmakers or the bipartisan state Ethics Commission ever previously digging into his claims. He argued the Democratic-led administration and Legislature have shown no interest in investigating corruption.
Leaning into his background as a federal investigator, Charles pushed for the release of records and communications to verify denials from Pingree, who during a debate last week called the allegations “made up.”
The Democrat has said she was not involved in the $840,000 award. It came as part of a MaineHousing initiative to finance new or rehabilitated rentals in Maine’s island communities. Pingree chaired the North Haven Sustainable Housing board in a volunteer capacity and received no financial compensation for the role, her campaign said.
The Island Institute said Charles’ claims about the $38,000 grant were false, saying it was used to enroll three other island communities in a state climate program.
“Restricted grants from foundations funded Island Institute’s Climate of Change film produced in 2022 as well as other films in the series,” Sue McKechnie, the group’s chief marketing and philanthropy officer, said Tuesday. “No federal or state dollars were used by Island Institute for this film series.”
The Pingree campaign blasted the claims and the exhibit as misinformation from the Republican’s flailing bid, using a statement to continue linking Charles with President Donald Trump.
“This is a desperate stunt built on baseless allegations that the media, state government and Hannah Pingree have already knocked down,” spokesperson Mary-Erin Casale said. “It’s also straight out of the Trump playbook: invent smears about your opponent so no one asks about your own record.”
Pingree’s campaign, as well as independent state Sen. Rick Bennett of Oxford, has described Charles as a “career lobbyist” despite his pledges to be bought by no one.
In Bangor, an interactive kids station featured puzzles crafted out of documents signed by Pingree when she was state House speaker, blank coloring sheets painting Pingree and Mills as “the faces of Maine’s corruption,” and bowls of candy under photos of the candidates: Smarties for Charles and Dum-Dums for Pingree.
Asked about accusations from Democrats that he’s chosen to go negative in the final stretch instead of focusing on issues, Charles launched into priorities he’d address if elected, including tax relief, education overhauls, cutting energy costs and targeting fraud, and improved substance abuse and rehabilitation programs. But he turned back to “Pingree’s corruption.”
“When we open the books on [Pingree’s] make-believe office, we’re going to find there’s a lot more there,” he said.

Medicare Advantage plans in Maine are being canceled, but new ones are being offered
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Shoshana Hoose was surprised to see a letter in the mail last week informing her that her Martin’s Point Medicare Advantage plan for 2027 was canceled.
Hoose, 72, a Portland retiree, said she has to start looking for another plan — a complicated task during Medicare’s open enrollment, which began Thursday and runs through Dec. 7.
“Exactly how this is going to play out for me I have no idea,” Hoose said. “I have a doctor’s appointment in January, and I don’t know who is going to be paying for it.”
Martin’s Point will have 41,528 Medicare Advantage plan terminations for 2027, representing 63% of its plans, according to an October edition of the Medicare Markets Insight newsletter. That’s the 14th-highest percentage of plan terminations by an insurance carrier nationwide, according to the newsletter.
Steve Amendo, a spokesperson for Martin’s Point, said in an emailed statement on Tuesday that while some plans are being canceled, new ones are being placed on the market.
“While these members are enrolled in plans that won’t be offered in 2027, we have introduced new plans in their place, and are communicating directly with impacted members to help them understand their options and, where appropriate, enroll in a new Martin’s Point plan for 2027,” Amendo said.
Amendo said Martin’s Point will continue to sell Medicare Advantage plans in all of Maine’s counties. In addition to being a Medicare Advantage insurer, Portland-based Martin’s Point is a primary and specialty care provider.
Medicare Advantage is insurance that’s an alternative to traditional Medicare, which is health care for those 65 and older. Under Medicare Advantage, enrollees often receive perks, such as gym memberships, dental and vision coverage, that are unavailable in traditional Medicare.
The Maine Bureau of Insurance, in an email to the Portland Press Herald on Tuesday, reported that a total of 49,297 Medicare Advantage plans are being discontinued statewide for 2027, including plans by Martin’s Point, UnitedHealth Group and Centene Corporation.
About 40,000 plans were canceled in Maine for 2026, according to the state insurance bureau, which said Maine has about 199,000 Medicare Advantage enrollees this year.
Nationally, nearly 3.2 million Medicare Advantage plans have been canceled for 2027, according to Medicare Market Insights.
Mitchell Stein, a Maine-based health policy consultant, said in an interview on Monday that changes the Biden administration made to Medicare Advantage plans in an effort to reign in costs have caused ballooning cancellations across the country.
The Biden administration cracked down on Medicare Advantage overpayments in 2023, working to recover improper payments, according to news reports.
Stein said Medicare Advantage insurers responded by canceling plans.
“They have cut back on benefits to bring their services more in line with traditional Medicare,” Stein said.
Medicare Advantage also saves money for insurers by designing narrower healthcare provider networks, so customers will still retain some of the perks, like dental and vision. Stein said the plans will likely offer fewer benefits or require more out-of-pocket charges for patients.
Traditional Medicare has a wide network that includes most healthcare providers.
Amendo said Medicare Advantage customers who need help can contact Martin’s Point.
“We recognize that changes to health plan coverage can raise questions for members, and we are committed to being there for them every step of the way,” Amendo said.

CINCINNATI (WXIX/Gray News) - An investigation is underway after a crane operator working the Brent Spence Bridge Corridor Project construction zone died over the weekend.
According to the Cincinnati Police Department, officers were called on Saturday morning to the West Third Street and Pete Rose Way area for a workplace accident.
The man was operating a boom lift crane when the crane shifted and fell, police explained.
The worker, who was not immediately identified by officials, was injured and taken to the University of Cincinnati Medical Center. However, he did not survive.
The Criminal Investigation Section and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration are investigating.
The Ohio Department of Transportation said the man was a Walsh-Kokosing crew member.
“We are saddened by the loss of a Walsh-Kokosing crew member while operating equipment at a Brent Spence Bridge Corridor project job site in Ohio,” a department spokesperson shared. “We offer sincere condolences to their loved ones and colleagues. We take the safety of everyone working on this major project seriously.”
Walsh-Kokosing Joint Venture is the main contractor for the Brent Spence Bridge Corridor Project.
The project is described as a multi-billion-dollar infrastructure effort designed to relieve traffic congestion, improve safety, and upgrade portions of Interstate 71 and Interstate 75 spanning across the Ohio River between Covington, Kentucky, and Cincinnati.

title: Republican PAC airs Troy Jackson attack ad; Susan Collins’ campaign calls for it to be taken down
text:
A new attack ad from a Republican political action committee has hit Maine’s airwaves and is already facing calls for it to “be taken down immediately.”
The 60-second ad in the form of a song attacking Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson, which starts with a piano riff followed by country music, began making the rounds on social media Tuesday. The chorus includes the line, “If he’ll screw his own family, he’ll screw yours, too.”
Troy Jackson and his partner are reportedly second cousins, which means they share a great-grandparent. Their relationship is legal across the country.
The ad was funded by the Republican-supporting Senate Leadership Fund PAC. It was not immediately clear how much money the SLF put behind the radio ad. But according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact, the group’s radio buy for all ads for the month of October so far eclipsed $405,000 as of Tuesday.
Shawn Roderick, a spokesperson for Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign, called for the ad to “be taken down immediately” on Tuesday.
“Senator Collins believes there have been far too many personal attacks in this campaign,” Roderick said in a written statement. “This ad has nothing to do with Troy Jackson’s qualifications for the job and should be taken down immediately.”
Jackson’s campaign called on Collins to apologize for the ad.
“If Collins believes these attacks are wrong, she owes Troy’s family an apology for spreading them herself and must take responsibility for her allies pushing the same personal attack on his family on TV right now,” Jackson campaign spokesman Dan Gottlieb said in an email late Tuesday. “Mainers deserve a debate about their futures, not a campaign dragging a family through the mud.”
Collins had been asked about Jackson’s personal life in an interview with Politico that was released on Sept 2.
Politico’s Jonathan Martin asked Collins if the circumstances of Jackson’s “personal life and the mother of his children (should) be relevant to this campaign.”
“Well, I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” Collins said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not. … It’s not something I’m going to be emphasizing.”
No state in the U.S. prohibits people from marrying their second cousin; Jackson and his partner are not married.
Spokespeople for the SLF did not respond Tuesday night to a request for comment on the ad or the calls by Collins’ campaign to take it down.

Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey spares death row inmate, citing doubts about evidence
text:
MONTGOMERY, Ala. (AP) — Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey on Tuesday commuted the death sentence of a death-row inmate after a number of former public officials, and the current district attorney, raised doubts about his conviction.
The Republican governor said she was commuting Toforest Johnson’s death sentence to life in prison without parole. Johnson was convicted of the 1995 murder of Jefferson County Deputy Sheriff William Hardy. Johnson has long maintained he is innocent.
“When presented with Mr. Johnson’s case, I had concerns there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment, death,” Ivey said in a statement. “My decision is not a determination of innocence, but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence to life imprisonment, without possibility of parole.”
Ivey has overseen 27 executions during her time as governor. She has commuted the death sentence of three death row inmates.
Hardy was shot twice in the head while working off-duty security at a hotel. Johnson has maintained he was on the other side of town at the time of the shooting.
Ty Alper, one of Toforest Johnson’s attorneys, said they are grateful to Ivey for “diligently reviewing Toforest’s case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution.” Alper said the fight to overturn the conviction will continue.
“Toforest Johnson is innocent. Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family,” Alper said.
There has been a long-running legal effort to win a new trial in the case that has garnered national attention and was the subject of a podcast. Jefferson County District Attorney Danny Carr, who was elected in 2018, has supported Johnson’s bid for a new trial. Carr wrote in a 2024 court filing that the “evidence in this case has unraveled over 20 years.”
Carr said in 2024 that credible alibi witnesses place Johnson elsewhere at the time of the crime. He said there are multiple reasons to doubt the key prosecution witness, a woman who “claimed she overheard Johnson confess to the murder on a three-way phone call on which she was eavesdropping.”
The key prosecution witness at Johnson’s 1998 trial testified that, while eavesdropping on a phone call, she heard a man she believed was Johnson admitting to the crime. She was paid $5,000 in 2001 for her testimony, and Johnson’s lawyers argue that the state withheld evidence of monetary motivation for the testimony.
A number of former judges and prosecutors have joined those seeking a new trial for Johnson amid questions about his conviction more than 20 years ago. Former Alabama Attorney General Bill Baxley, former Chief Justices Sonny Hornsby and Drayton Nabers, and several former judges and prosecutors have submitted briefs or written editorials supporting a new trial.

Florida puts 77-year-old man to death for deputy’s killing in its 18th execution this year
text:
STARKE, Fla. (AP) — Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis ’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.
William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the September 1986 shooting death of Indian River County sheriff’s deputy Richard Raczkoski.
The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6 p.m. execution time with Reaves already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last words, he replied ”No, I do not.”
The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and shouted his name, but there was no response. A medic was called in a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.
Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a year, and it’s poised to tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.
DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said he wants justice to be delivered to victims’ families who have often waited decades for death sentences to be imposed.
Marc Raczkoski, the deputy’s brother, briefly told reporters after witnessing the execution that his brother finally got justice.
But Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who was also on hand, said at a post-execution briefing that he saw the execution as closure, not justice.
“Would we all be so lucky to be 77 years old and to die so peacefully,” Flowers said. “That’s not justice in any way in my opinion.”
Reaves struggled with the deputy after dropping a gun
Raczkoski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store on Sept. 23, 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.
While the two men talked, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. They then struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. Raczkoski died later that day from his wounds.
Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and newly sentenced to death in 1992. Subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.
The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ 11th-hour appeal without comment.
Lawyers challenged lethal injection procedure
The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals seeking to spare his life.
His attorneys challenged Florida’s three-drug lethal injection protocol. All Florida executions are carried out via injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.
The court has previously upheld the protocol against similar challenges. Florida’s method differs from the single-drug injection used in states such as Tennessee, where condemned inmate Christa Pike was rushed to a hospital last month after surviving two doses of pentobarbital.
Reaves’ attorneys also argued that jurors who recommended the death penalty were never told the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs had rated the Army veteran as 100% disabled because of post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from his service in the Vietnam War.
More than 100 military veterans appealed to DeSantis to halt the execution in a letter Monday, citing those factors.
Florida close to tying its 2025 record of 19 executions
A total of 47 people were executed in the United States in 2025. Florida led the nation that year with 19 executions and has accounted for more than half of the 32 U.S. executions — Reaves included — carried out thus far in 2026.
In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, becoming the first state in nearly a decade to do so.
On Nov. 5, Jesse Guardado, 64, is scheduled to receive a lethal injection in the same Florida death chamber. Guardado was convicted of robbing and killing a 75-year-old woman while stealing items on a crack cocaine binge in 2004.

Plan to expand Juniper Ridge Landfill advances following Superior Court decision
text:
The state’s plan to expand its largest landfill advanced after a Penobscot County Superior Court judge denied an appeal of the Maine Department of Environmental Protection’s go-ahead for the project.
The Penobscot Nation and the Conservation Law Foundation have been fighting to block a 61-acre expansion of the Juniper Ridge Landfill in Old Town, which is located just northwest of the Penobscot River and the tribe’s reservation islands.
The foundation and Penobscot Nation say they are reviewing the ruling and evaluating next steps.
The expansion would add 12 million cubic yards of capacity to the facility, which currently handles a little more than half of Maine’s landfilled waste.
In October 2024, the Maine DEP decided the proposal met the state’s public benefit criteria for expansion. Under Maine law, a public benefit assessment is a mandatory review intended to ensure that landfill expansions provide a clear advantage to the state without unfairly targeting a specific population.
But months later, lawyers for the foundation and tribe filed a petition asking a judge to revisit the public benefit determination. Tribal leaders and neighbors of the landfill have complained about noxious odors, fires and other environmental risks it may pose
A judge overturned the DEP’s first public benefit determination in January, ordering the agency to more thoroughly consider the cumulative harms to the tribe. The matter returned to court in July.
The foundation said in a news release Tuesday that a judge upheld Maine DEP’s approval of the project.
“We have fought pollution, injustice, and decades of harm to heal the Penobscot River, a relative that has sustained our people since time immemorial and continues to sustain communities across Maine,” Penobscot Nation Tribal Chief Kirk E. Francis said in the news release. “We are not asking the state to undo generations of harm overnight. We are asking it not to take us backward.
“Our cultural survival is tied to the health of the Penobscot River, and there is too much at stake to keep adding to the harms it already carries.”
Alex St. Pierre, the Conservation Law Foundation’s vice president for environmental justice, described the ruling as “a setback,” and said “it can’t bury” the concerns the Penobscot Nation and area residents have raised.
“The knowledge, persistence, and power of these communities have already shifted the conversation – and that momentum will carry forward until justice is served,” St. Pierre said in the news release.
A spokesperson for the DEP did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday evening.
Staff Writer Penelope Overton contributed to this story.

Two severely malnourished dogs were discovered inside a Knox County residence during a probation check that led to a Camden man's arrest on a felony firearm charge, according to court documents.
Seth M. Young, 28, was arrested on Oct. 15 and charged with possession of a firearm by a prohibited person, a Class B felony.
According to a narrative filed by the Knox County Sheriff's Deputy, the investigation began when deputies observed suspicious activity involving two vehicles at Andes Variety in Warren.
Deputies later followed a blue Subaru and conducted a traffic stop after noticing the registration had expired.
During the stop, deputies learned that Young, who was a passenger in the car, was on probation with search conditions related to drugs.
Court documents say that deputies accompanied Young to a residence in Spruce Head to conduct a probation check.
During the check, deputies reported encountering an overwhelming smell of feces and discovered two dogs confined in separate cages, according to the deputy's narrative.
Both dogs were described as malnourished, with their bones visible. Deputies also reported finding a large accumulation of dog feces inside one of the cages.
Pope Memorial Humane Society confirmed on Tuesday that both dogs are now in its care.
Deputies also reported finding a double-barrel shotgun and ammunition inside the residence.
The deputy's report indicated that additional charges related to the dogs' welfare could be considered. Court documents do not show any animal cruelty charges filed against Young.
Young was transported to Knox County Jail following his arrest, according to court documents. His bail was set at $2,500 cash, with conditions prohibiting him from possessing firearms or other dangerous weapons.
Young is scheduled to appear in person for a dispositional conference Nov. 13 at 8:30 a.m. at the Knox County Courthouse in Rockland.

President Donald Trump announced a new initiative to combat U.S. taxpayer fraud, offering financial rewards to those who provide tips leading to successful fraud convictions or significant federal actions.
The Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, or WHIP for short, was launched by President Trump and Vice President JD Vance during an Oval Office event Tuesday. The $25 million program, administered by the Department of Justice, promises rewards of up to $30,000 for actionable information.

Yarmouth boys soccer pulls away from Greely, secures top seed in B South
text:
YARMOUTH — For a 10-minute stretch to start the second half, the Greely boys soccer team showed it could make the top team in Class B South very uncomfortable.
Then the defending champions from Yarmouth showed how they’ve been absolutely steamrolling the competition for the past month.
The Clippers scored four goals in response to a quick-strike tying goal by the Rangers and pulled away for 5-1 win Tuesday in their final regular-season game.
It was Yarmouth’s 10th straight win. During that run, the Clippers have scored five or more goals eight times and outscored their opponents 63-4. Yarmouth will be the top seed in B South with a 12-1-1 record.
“A lot of it is our response to the loss we had,” said center back Owen Advani, referencing a setback at Fryeburg Academy on Sept. 17. “As a team, we’ve been working in practice emphasizing trying to get better.”
Greely coach Mike Andreasen said his now 8-5-1 Rangers should stay at No. 3 and also receive a first-round bye. Both teams will begin their playoff quest hosting a regional quarterfinal, scheduled to be played on Oct. 28.
YARMOUTH’S APPROACH
Clippers coach Justin Morrill praised his team’s ability and willingness to move the ball calmly and crisply.
It was evident, particularly in the first half, by how well and comfortably Advani and fellow center back and captain Finn Grimes played with the ball at their feet. Often with help from goalie Gabriel Janczuk, Advani and Grimes worked the ball left-and-right to outside backs Joel Butler, Cael Woelflein, Landon Brewer and Will Ahrens. When Greely would press forward, the pass was sent forward to start the Yarmouth attack.
“I think it’s been unique because we have a good solid group of four in the back that we’re all confident with the ball at our feet,” said Advani, a senior captain with Grimes.
Lucas Hayner scored the Clippers’ first two goals, a first-half tally off a nice pass by Butler and then a rebound put-away on a Tate MacVane shot that put Yarmouth back in front with 29:22 to play.
“Tate did all the work. He dribbled around like four people,” Hayner said.
Trevor Hunt’s goal that made it 3-1 with 6:51 to play was the prettiest of the game. Hunt leapt up and one-timed a long cross from Cole MacVane to the back post, a sequence that started out of the back with a pass by Woelflein.
Greely then went to its bench. Yarmouth added tallies from Brewer and Garcia Eduardo (a header off a Woeflein cross).
GREELY GAINING CONFIDENCE?
Greely earned a 1-1 tie against Yarmouth when the teams met in the second game of the season.
When Gavin Byrne played a quick pass ahead to Ethan King, and King chipped a shot over Janczuk, the Rangers had reversed the field in seconds and tied it Tuesday with 31:55 to play. A minute into the half, Janczuk had to make a diving stop on Johan Clorius. After Hayner’s second goal, Logan Emerson had a pair of chances to tie it up a second time.
“My big question to the kids after the game was, ‘Do we think we can beat this team?'” Andreasen said. “And they said, ‘Yeah.’ We played a good second half, we had some good chances. The last two goals … they are what they are.”

Maine Hospice Council in Augusta closes after 35 years
text:
The Maine Hospice Council announced this week it was ceasing operations after more than four decades of advocacy, training and education to address local gaps in hospice care.
The Augusta-based organization connected individuals with hospice centers and pioneered a number of programs to improve access to end-of-life care in Maine, including the Hospice Veteran Partnership and Maine Pain Initiative, according to a Tuesday news release.
“This decision was not made lightly,” Alicia Murray, board president, said in the release. “We are incredibly proud of the impact our organization has made and deeply grateful to everyone who supported our mission. While closing our doors is difficult, we celebrate the lives touched, the relationships built, and the lasting contributions made to our community.”
Since its founding in 1984, the Maine Hospice Council has been the state’s leading advocate for end-of-life care. It secured annual funding from the state and nonprofit status by 1990, which, along with grants, donations, membership dues and other funding sources, supported more than three decades of operations.
The Maine Hospice Council received $127,012 from the state for fiscal year 2025 and $63,506 the next two years. Murray said the organization shuttered due to “lack of regular revenue stream.”
“They’ve actually done a really good job to work with very little regular revenue for as long as they have,” she said.
The council’s achievements include developing the Maine State Prison’s comprehensive hospice program and a handful of policies to improve the quality of end-of-life care and establish standards for hospice program licensure. The group also advocated for better delivery of palliative care, medical care that relieves symptoms and pain caused by serious illness.
Kandyce Powell, the council’s executive director, said she would continue to be available to anyone searching for end-of-life resources.
The closure comes amid rising demand for age-related services. Maine’s 65 and older population is expected to grow by more than 20% by 2032, while the direct care workforce is already short 2,000 employees.

Polymarket removes contract allowing users to wager on fate of Cornell students accused of rape
text:
Polymarket has removed a contract from its prediction market platform that allowed users to wager on whether any of the seven men accused of raping a Cornell student in 2024 will be charged with a felony sex crime.
The market was made available on Sept. 30 and was slated to close on Jan. 31. It had more than $450,000 in volume before it was taken off Polymarket’s international platform. The company’s U.S. exchange is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which bans trading related to “activity that is unlawful under Federal or State law.”
“Our primary goal at Polymarket is to bring objective, data-driven insight to the most important questions of our time,” a Polymarket spokesperson said Tuesday. “This market addressed whether the government would take action — a process that deserves scrutiny, particularly in a case of such serious concern. That said, we believe in the wisdom of crowds, have heard them loud and clear, and removed the market.”
Front Office Sports was the first to report on the contract.
Some outcry over the Polymarket contract has been aimed at its celebrity promoters. Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has an endorsement deal with Polymarket, and he recently appeared in a star-studded commercial that also included cameos by Derek Jeter, Eli Manning, Sue Bird and several celebrities.
Messages were left by the AP on Tuesday with representatives for James, Jeter, Manning and Bird.
Polymarket also has partnership agreements with the NHL, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, the UFC and ATP Tour. Messages were left by the AP seeking comment from each organization.
A spokesman for Spike Lee, who also appeared in the Polymarket commercial with James, said the director had no comment. Messages also were left with representatives for actors Craig Robinson, John Leguizamo and Alexandra Daddario — who were also part of the commercial with James.
A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either that their interactions were consensual or that they weren’t involved.
Online critics characterized the Polymarket contract as degrading and questioned why celebrity ambassadors would associate themselves with the company. An online petition singled out James, Manning, Daddario and model Emily Ratajkowski while calling on other famous endorsers to cut ties with the company.
Prediction markets provide an opportunity to trade on the result of future events. Sports account for a major portion of the volume generated by the array of typically yes-or-no question, depending on the platform.
When a U.S. Army sergeant was indicted earlier this year over bets on the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, he was trading on Polymarket’s international platform. The Associated Press reported in April that 50 brand new accounts on Polymarket’s international platform placed substantial bets on a U.S.-Iran ceasefire in the hours, even minutes, before President Donald Trump announced a ceasefire on social media, raising concerns of insider trading.
Polymarket had an active market on its international platform on Tuesday that allowed customers to trade on whether Cornell president Michael Kotlikoff will be out by Oct. 31. It had more than $10,700 in volume.

NFL defends Eagles’ handling of Jalen Hurts’ blood clots while union calls for investigation
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The NFL staunchly defended the Philadelphia Eagles’ handling of quarterback Jalen Hurts’ blood clots on Tuesday, while hours later the players’ union called for an investigation of the situation.
A person with knowledge of the situation confirmed to The Associated Press that the Eagles were not being disciplined for their actions with Hurts. The person spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because conversations between the league and team were to remain private.
Dr. Allen Sills, the NFL’s chief medical officer, offered a passionate defense of how the Eagles treated Hurts, following a statement from the league that said officials had been in contact with Philadelphia’s medical personnel and the Cleveland Clinic in London throughout the process.
“I have complete confidence in the Eagles’ medical staff and their handling of this situation, and I would characterize their work as very conservative, very patient-focused and appropriately guarded at every step,” Sills said at the league’s annual fall meeting. “I don’t think you can take that outcome and say there was something flawed about the process. Sometimes in medicine, we do all the right things and diseases progress and other things develop. ...
“In this case, everyone was incredibly conservative and incredibly vigilant and was very quick to make diagnoses of these conditions that might not have been diagnosed in a nonathlete.”
The NFL Players Association in a statement said it was told by the league that a review was not planned.
“Before conclusions are drawn about how this situation was handled, there must be a full investigation into what occurred,” the union said. “Determining the facts is essential to ensuring players receive the highest level of care and protection going forward.”
Hurts is on injured reserve and expected to miss the rest of the season after a blood clot in his left calf traveled to his lungs. The Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said Monday that Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary embolisms.
NFL executive vice president Jeff Miller took issue with “uninformed speculation” in reports Monday that Hurts went more than 30 hours without sleep last weekend before playing.
“Jalen Hurts returned to the hotel, slept for a period of time and went to the stadium,” Miller said, estimating that Hurts slept for around seven or eight hours. “Both talking to the Eagles’ staff and making sure from people on the ground, tracking the case, talking to the independent hospital and doctors involved that we have, I think, a complete understanding of the course of events.”
Sills said the league and the players’ union study and track blood clots annually. He declined to go into specifics about Hurts’ condition, citing patient privacy, and reiterated multiple times that treating a blood clot involves looking at multiple factors.
Dr. Caron Rockman, a vascular surgeon for roughly 30 years, said based on what she has read, there’s no evidence the Eagles acted improperly while dealing with what she called not a textbook issue.
“It’s a judgment call,” said Rockman, who is currently a chair at Hackensack University Medical Center in New Jersey and did not treat Hurts. “I think it’s really a case-by-case basis. In my personal opinion, superficial vein thrombosis is not a (disqualification) to fly.”
Hurts’ treatment moving forward involves blood thinners, and he will not be allowed to participate in any football activities until he is off them.
Hurts played in London against Jacksonville on Oct. 11, three days after informing medical staff of the injury after practice. He was initially diagnosed by specialists in London with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis.
“I think there was incredible vigilance, there was conservative care, state-of-the-art imaging that was done in London,” Sills said. “And, as far as the timing and the decision-making, I have great confidence in that and believe that everyone acted with an abundance of caution.”
Sills in his opening statement that lasted more than five minutes said all decisions are made with medicine over football.
“The notion that there are external factors or that any of our physicians would put a player in harm’s way — that’s nonsense,” Sills said.
___
AP Sports Writer David Brandt in Phoenix and AP Pro Football Writer Rob Maaddi in Tampa, Florida, contributed to this report.

40-year-old wearing ‘old man’ mask charged in separate bank robberies
text:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (WWSB/Gray News) — A 40-year-old man has been charged with robbing two Florida banks, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Monday.
David Sartin Jr. of St. Petersburg, who has previously served time in prison for bank robbery in Texas, faces up to 20 years in federal prison on each count.
Court documents detail 2 robberies
According to court documents, Sartin allegedly robbed a bank in Largo on Aug. 24.
On Sept. 15, prosecutors said he robbed another bank in St. Petersburg.
During both robberies, Sartin entered the bank wearing a prosthetic “old man” mask, approached the teller counter and demanded money. He allegedly instructed the teller not to include dye packs.
Investigators believe Sartin parked his car near the bank, switched to a bicycle and approached the bank. After the robbery, Sartin fled on the bicycle, retrieved the vehicle and drove away.
Video surveillance of the suspect’s home captured footage of a white male resembling Sartin unloading a bicycle from the vehicle and rolling it toward the residence. The next day, investigators observed Sartin spray-paint the vehicle’s white roof black, making the entire vehicle appear dark in color.
Searches turn up disguise items
A search of Sartin’s home uncovered a bicycle, a blue suit and a black bag, all similar to the items used during the first robbery.
A search of Sartin’s storage unit revealed a backpack and laptop bag containing the mask with gray facial hair, dark-framed glasses and work gloves with black paint on them. The bags also contained a fake handgun and clothing consistent with the disguise worn during the second robbery.
Agents also searched another house where Sartin occasionally stayed. They found several items, including a prosthetic mask different from the one used in the robberies and a journal titled, “God’s Best friend is a Bank Robber! Uncle Henry Cops and Robbers the world through the eyes of a Bank Robber.”
The journal was dated “Jan. 1, 2021,” and was “written by: David Sartin.”
Prior convictions
Sartin was on supervised release for a 2018 federal conviction stemming from five bank robberies he had committed, also using a mask, in Texas in 2016.
In 2008, Sartin was convicted of attempted bank robbery after he and a co-conspirator had tried to rob a bank wearing Halloween masks and disguises.

Jackson seeks to unseat longtime incumbent Collins in Senate race
text:
Troy Jackson seeks to unseat longtime Sen. Susan Collins in Maine's Senate race
Mainers have spent most of the election cycle watching Troy Jackson campaign to be governor, but now he’s aiming to be Maine’s next U.S. senator.
Just a few months ago, Jackson was selected to try to unseat incumbent Sen. Susan Collins with about three months to campaign. He replaced Graham Platner after Platner dropped out due to a sexual assault allegation he denies.
“I didn't think it was going to be me,” Jackson said. “I'd have been happy to go along, be part of, you know, this push to change our government, but the fact that now I'm in this position is really exciting for me.”
Jackson is a fifth-generation logger and spent 20 years in Augusta as a legislator, including six years as state Senate president. He’s also a union man.
“When you stand together as a group of people, you have solidarity, you have strength,” Jackson said. “You know that you have other people that are going through the same thing, and it gives you more ability to stand up, be hopeful, be strong.”
Jackson hails from Aroostook County and recently became a grandfather to a baby girl.
"What kind of Maine is that baby girl and other babies across the state going to grow up in?" Jackson said.
Democrats nationwide and Jackson seek to flip the Senate majority down in Washington. To help Democrats reach their goal, Jackson will have to beat Collins, who has held the seat for nearly three decades and is seeking a sixth term.
If Jackson succeeds, Maine will lose Collins’ power as the chair of the Senate appropriations committee, which has brought the state millions of dollars in federal funding. Jackson has spent a large part of his campaign attempting to tie Collins to President Donald Trump. He also says she has no pull as appropriations chair.
“It doesn't do you any good to be chair of appropriations if you don't use that chair to actually leverage it in a way that actually helps the state,” Jackson said.
If Jackson and his party are successful, they will have to find a way to work with President Trump, who is hoping Republicans keep their Senate majority.
Jackson says voters have already seen him work across the aisle, pointing to his time working with Republican Governor Paul LePage.
“I'm not going to let personal animosity get in the way of doing whatever I can to help move this state forward,” Jackson said.
Since the start of his Senate campaign, Jackson has been met with some flak from his opponents, including criticism of his son's lobbying and allegedly benefitting from Jackson while he was still in the Legislature.
“Things about my son and stuff like that are just not true, but I think it just goes to show how desperate they are,” Jackson said.
Jackson has also been criticized for allegedly throwing a water bottle at a colleague in 2021. He denies those allegations.
If he gets his chance in Washington, Jackson says his top priority will be healthcare. He’s advocating universal healthcare and says he wants everyone to have affordable services.
“People keep this narrative that we can't do Medicare for all because it won't be as good of a system, that it’s a problem,” Jackson said. “I haven't had a Canadian tell me that they don't like their healthcare system, and I've worked with them for years.”
Ahead of Election Day, Jackson says he wants voters who want change to elect someone who cares.
“Do you like the government we're in right now? I mean, I don't,” Jackson said. “It’s not a Democrat or Republican thing. It's just the idea that this government is not working for everyone I care about.”
Jackson and Collins go head-to-head on Nov. 3.

(Gray News) - Racing legend Fred Lorenzen became the first NASCAR driver to officially be diagnosed with chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE.
The Concussion and CTE Foundation announced that Lorenzen suffered from stage 3 CTE before his death in 2024 at 89. According to the foundation’s press release, Lorenzen lived with dementia for the last 20 years of his life.
“My dad struggled for many years, long before he was diagnosed with dementia in his 60s,” his daughter, Amanda Lorenzen Gardstrom, said. “Watching him go through that, and experiencing the impact it had on me and our family was incredibly difficult and beyond heartbreaking.”
It was only through research on Lorenzen’s brain at Boston University after his death that medical officials were able to confirm the CTE diagnosis.
There is currently no way to test for CTE until after death.
Lorenzen said in 2016 that he would donate his brain for research following his death, according to Motorsport. Dale Earnhardt Jr. has also previously said he would donate his brain.
Lorenzen’s family has donated about $1 million to the Concussion and CTE Foundation to fund further CTE research. The donation also helped establish the Fred Lorenzen Memorial Helpline, which will help connect drivers and their families with “care navigation, education, and support groups.”
“While he may be the first race car driver diagnosed with CTE, we know from outreach to other drivers that he isn’t the only one suffering. I know there are so many more out there who need help,” Lorenzen Gardstrom said. “Our family wants to honor our dad’s legacy by making sure other drivers and their families have help navigating this devastating disease and hopefully better answers in the future.”
According to the press release, Lorenzen’s family contacted NASCAR following the diagnosis in hopes the organization would join their efforts in researching CTE among drivers. However, NASCAR declined and has played no part in their efforts.
“My dad’s dementia care came at a significant financial and emotional cost to our family,” Chris Lorenzen said. “We had hoped NASCAR would join us in this effort, and while we’re disappointed that hasn’t happened, we remain hopeful there will be opportunities to work together to support the drivers who helped build the sport.”
Lorenzen had 26 victories in the NASCAR Cup Series during his 158-race career, according to Sports Illustrated. He won the Daytona 500 in 1965 and the World 600 (now known as the Coca-Cola 600) in 1963 and 1965.
In 2015, Lorenzen was inducted into the NASCAR Hall of Fame.

Mom arrested after allegedly crashing car into telephone pole while drunk with child in back seat
text:
DAVENPORT, Iowa (KWQC/Gray News) - An Iowa woman is facing several charges after authorities say she crashed her car with her child inside while drunk on Monday.
According to court documents, Kayla M. Delay, 36, is facing charges that include child endangerment resulting in bodily injury, having an open container, operating while intoxicated and possessing a controlled substance.
Davenport authorities said Delay was taken into custody after police responded that evening to a reported crash on Rockingham Road involving a vehicle that had collided with a telephone pole.
A witness told police that Delay was seen walking away from the crash with her child.
Once police located Delay, they noted seeing bruising and swelling on the child’s face. Court documents showed the child’s nose was also bleeding.
The child was taken to the hospital for treatment.
Officers at the scene reported that Delay was unsteady while walking and smelled like alcohol when they were speaking to her about what happened. They also said she had slurred speech, bloodshot and watery eyes.
Court documents stated that Delay admitted to driving the vehicle and that her child was in the back seat at the time of the crash.
Police said they found an open container of alcohol in the vehicle and a THC vape pen in her purse.
She refused a field sobriety test and a breathalyzer, court documents stated.
The 36-year-old mother was booked into Scott County Jail on Monday before bonding out before midnight.

Patriots safety Kevin Byard looking forward to facing former team
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — New England Patriots safety Kevin Byard doesn’t have any hard feelings about the two seasons he spent with the Chicago Bears.
But this week he is trying to think of any tips to help his new team walk out of its game Thursday in Chicago with a victory against his former team.
“I’m giving the coaches and the players as much as I can, you know what I mean?” Byard said on Tuesday. “Obviously, I am not there anymore, and I don’t have all my notes and stuff like that. But as far as personnel, anything I can kind of remember.”
Byard experienced plenty during his two seasons with the Bears.
He arrived in 2024 after his lone season in Philadelphia, signed a two-year deal and was selected as a captain on his new team. He then proceeded to be part of a rebuilding year that included coach Matt Eberflus being fired after 12 games in what ended up being a 10-game losing streak.
The Bears quickly turned things around last season under new coach Ben Johnson, and Byard thrived in the new environment, leading the NFL in interceptions while being selected as an All-Pro for the third time in his career.
It’s why the main feeling he’s taking with him when he returns to Soldier Field this week is one of respect.
“Definitely excited to go back to Chicago and play up there,” Byard said. “I loved playing in that stadium in front of those fans. It’s going to be an electric environment.”
Part of Byard’s experience over the past two seasons was getting to know Bears quarterback Caleb Williams, who was his fellow captain both years.
Williams said he learned a lot from Byard during their time together.
“Obviously, being able to go versus him, practice for two years. I mean, he’s a super savvy vet,” Williams said. “I know he’s getting up there in age (laughs), but he’s still fast, and he does — I’ve seen him work. He studies film. He still moves extremely well. He knows the route concepts really well.”
It’s given the Patriots an extra lift to a secondary that already includes star Christian Gonzalez.
Johnson isn’t surprised that Byard has fit in so well in New England’s locker room.
“I love Kevin Byard and what he brings to the table. You can tell he really fits their defense well in terms of the communication and what they’re asking him to do,” Johnson said.
Though Byard has yet to intercept a pass through the Patriots first six games, Williams said he’ll be keeping an eye on him this week.
“It’s gonna be a great challenge for us, a great challenge for me and the wide receivers to be able to go out there and execute and complete passes and keep being the offense and identity that we wanna be,” Williams said.
Byard said the respect is mutual.
“I love his mentality, I’m a huge fan of him, honestly,” Byard said. “I just think the care, his willingness to go out there and fight every day with his team. So I’m excited to play against him and hopefully our defense can have a better day.”

Celtics blow 22-point lead, lose opener to Pistons
text:
DETROIT — Javonte Green scored 19 points after not playing in the first half and Cade Cunningham finished with 22 points and eight assists, helping the Detroit Pistons come back and beat the Boston Celtics 121-113 on Tuesday.
The NBA picked the matinee matchup to tip off the season and it delivered plenty of entertainment.
Paul George scored 38 points, the most by a Celtic in his debut. The nine-time All-Star, in his 17th season, showed he’s still got it in his first game with Boston since it acquired him from Philadelphia in exchange for 2024 NBA Finals MVP Jaylen Brown.
Jayson Tatum, though, was off his game. He missed 17 of 23 shots had 13 points and 11 assists. His lack of hustle on defense allowed Green to take his time for a fifth 3-pointer that gave the Pistons a 13-point lead with 3:33 left.
Tatum, a six-time All-Star, is set to play his first full season since tearing his Achilles tendon in May 2025.
Boston took its biggest lead early in the third quarter at 72-50 after George made three 3-pointers in less than a minute.
Detroit cut its deficit to six points after three quarters and surged ahead in the fourth. Green made a go-ahead 3, Duren added a three-point play and Robinson connected on a 3 to put the Pistons ahead 107-99 with 5:10 to go.
Jalen Duren had 22 points and nine rebounds, Duncan Robinson scored 21 points — making 5 of 9 3-pointers — and Ausar Thompson added 11 points and 11 rebounds for the Pistons.
Boston’s Derrick White and Payton Pritchard scored 17 points apiece.
Up next
Celtics: Host the New York Knicks on Friday.
Pistons: At Miami on Friday.

Guatemalan man sentenced to 30 years for smuggling tragedy that killed 53 people in Texas
text:
A federal judge on Tuesday sentenced a Guatemalan man extradited to the U.S. over his role in a 2022 human smuggling attempt that ended in the deaths of 53 migrants who had been transported in a sweltering tractor-trailer in Texas.
U.S. and Guatemalan prosecutors called Rigoberto Román Miranda-Orozco’s sentencing another step toward justice in one of the deadliest smuggling attempts along the U.S.-Mexico border. Miranda-Orozco, 39, was sentenced to 30 years in prison after admitting to arranging travel and accommodations for two people who died and another who was seriously injured.
Nearly 20 people in the U.S. and Guatemala have been convicted since the discovery of the abandoned trailer full of bodies horrified communities accustomed to seeing their young people leave, trying to flee poverty or violence in Central America and Mexico.
“It was clear that they suffered tremendously in their last few hours on this earth,” U.S. Attorney Justin Simmons told reporters at a news conference following the sentencing.
People tried to ‘claw their way out’ of a tractor with no air conditioning
The trailer’s air conditioning malfunctioned and would not blow cool air to the people trapped inside during the sweltering, three-hour ride in June 2022 from the border city of Laredo to San Antonio, authorities said. Prosecutors have said migrants paid up to $15,000 each to be taken across the U.S. border.
When the abandoned trailer was opened on a remote San Antonio back road, 48 migrants were dead. Another 16 were taken to hospitals, where five more died.
Simmons said investigators found clothing passengers had shed to cool off and claw marks on the trailer’s walls.
“They were literally trying to claw their way out,” he said.
Twenty-one of those who died were from Guatemala, Simmons said.
Other defendants still await sentencing
U.S. District Judge Orlando Garcia sentenced Miranda-Orozco, who was arrested in Guatemala in 2024 and extradited to the U.S. the following year.
He pleaded guilty in July to conspiracy to bring a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, as well as aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in serious bodily injury, prosecutors said.
Simmons said prosecutors in Guatemala were integral in securing convictions for Miranda Orozco and others. Guatemalan Attorney Gabriel García Luna attended Tuesday’s news conference in Texas.
Last year, Felipe Orduna-Torres, described by prosecutors as the leader of the smuggling operations inside the U.S., was sentenced to life in prison in the U.S. Armando Gonzales-Ortega, his top assistant, was sentenced to 83 years.
Sentencing dates have been set for more people, including the truck’s driver.
The tragedy is the deadliest among those that have claimed thousands of lives in recent decades as people attempt to cross the U.S. border from Mexico. Ten migrants died in 2017 after they were trapped inside a truck parked at a Walmart in San Antonio.
In 2003, the bodies of 19 migrants were found in a sweltering truck southeast of San Antonio.
